candidate.answerReason: The prime roots must sum to 63, so one is the only even prime, 2, and the other is 61. This gives the single value k = 122.

methods.label: Use the parity of the root sum
methods.explanation:
Let the prime roots be \(p\) and \(q\). Expanding the monic quadratic with these roots gives
\[
(x-p)(x-q)=x^2-(p+q)x+pq.
\]
Comparing this with \(x^2-63x+k\) shows that
\[
p+q=63,\qquad k=pq.
\]
The sum is odd, so one root must be even and the other odd. The only even prime is \(2\), because every larger even integer has \(2\) as an additional factor. Thus the roots must be \(2\) and \(61\).

The number \(61\) is prime: a composite number below \(64\) must have a prime divisor among \(2,3,5,7\), and none divides \(61\). Therefore the pair is valid and gives
\[
k=2(61)=122.
\]
There is no other possible prime pair, and swapping the roots does not change their product. Hence there is \(\boxed{1}\) possible value of \(k\), choice B.
